x-e-m2-01.title: Fix the line with the wrong number in a beach cleanup blog post
x-e-m2-01.goal: Find the two number sentences in the blog post that don't match each other, and rewrite them to fit the confirmed information.
x-e-m2-01.material: A student in one class wrote this post on the school blog. (It is text only. Each line has a number.)
x-e-m2-01.thinking.0: Compare the information in the text to find a contradiction
x-e-m2-01.thinking.1: Decide which information needs to be checked
x-e-m2-01.prereq.0: Read easy English sentences (numbers and expressions like in total and first hour)
x-e-m2-01.s.s1.prompt: Pick the one line in this post that does not match the other sentences.
x-e-m2-01.s.s1.hint.0: Collect only the lines with numbers and compare them with each other.
x-e-m2-01.s.s1.explain: Line 3 says they collected 30 bags in the first hour, and line 4 says the total was 18 bags. The total cannot be less than what was collected in the first hour. This post alone cannot tell you whether line 3 or line 4 is wrong, so you may pick either one.
x-e-m2-01.s.s2.prompt: What is the best way for the writer to fix this error?
x-e-m2-01.s.s2.hint.0: First check whether the post tells you which of the two numbers is right.
x-e-m2-01.s.s2.hint.1: Think about where you could get the information to fix the wrong number.
x-e-m2-01.s.s2.explain: The post alone cannot tell you which of the two numbers is right. Checking with the people who counted the original number and fixing it to the correct one is the method with evidence. Changing it to 'a lot' also avoids the error, but it loses information.
x-e-m2-01.s.s3.prompt: Your friends checked, and the total was 30 bags. Rewrite lines 3 and 4 in English so the numbers match each other.
x-e-m2-01.s.s3.hint.1: Think about which sentence fits expressions like 'in total' or 'altogether'.
x-e-m2-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the total number smaller than the part number?
x-e-m2-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Do your two rewritten sentences avoid contradicting each other?
x-e-m2-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you keep 'the first hour' and 'the total' separate?
x-e-m2-01.s.s1.hint.1: Write down what each of the two lines with numbers is counting (over what time, up to where), and compare them side by side.
x-e-m2-01.s.s2.o.a: Check the actual numbers with the friends who counted the bags, and fix both lines together.
x-e-m2-01.s.s2.r.a: Asking the people who actually counted is a fix with a basis.
x-e-m2-01.s.s2.o.b: Change only the number in line 3 to less than 18, so the two lines agree with each other.
x-e-m2-01.s.s2.r.b: Even if the two numbers agree with each other, if they are not the values actually counted, the wrong information remains.
x-e-m2-01.s.s2.o.c: Write only "a lot" instead of a number, to remove the chance of being wrong.
x-e-m2-01.s.s2.r.c: The error disappears, but the information in the text disappears with it.
x-e-m2-01.s.s3.hint.0: First decide how many bags were collected in the first hour, and write that number next to the confirmed total of 30 bags to compare them.
x-e-m2-01.s.s3.modelNote.2: The number for the first hour can be anything as long as it is 30 or less.

x-e-m2-02.title: Infer what a bakery ad does not say
x-e-m2-02.goal: Tell apart inferences with evidence from guesses without evidence in an ad, and make a question about information the ad does not give.
x-e-m2-02.material:
This is an ad posted in front of a bakery.

Sweet Hill Bakery
Buy 2 muffins, get the third muffin free!
Today only. Our muffins are baked fresh every morning.
x-e-m2-02.thinking.0: Use evidence to tell inferences from guesses
x-e-m2-02.thinking.1: Find missing information and ask about it
x-e-m2-02.prereq.0: Read an easy English ad (buy, get, free, today only)
x-e-m2-02.s.s1.prompt: The ad does not say these things directly, but pick all the inferences you can believe from the ad alone.
x-e-m2-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each choice, point to the sentence in the ad it comes from.
x-e-m2-02.s.s1.o.a: Today, if you buy 3 muffins, you pay for only 2.
x-e-m2-02.s.s1.r.a: This is a conclusion that follows when you work out the sentence in the ad.
x-e-m2-02.s.s1.o.b: The same deal will be offered tomorrow too.
x-e-m2-02.s.s1.r.b: This guess directly contradicts the words 'Today only'.
x-e-m2-02.s.s1.o.c: If you buy only 1 muffin, there is no free muffin.
x-e-m2-02.s.s1.r.c: This is an inference from reading the condition 'if you buy 2'.
x-e-m2-02.s.s1.o.d: This bakery's muffins are cheaper than other bakeries'.
x-e-m2-02.s.s1.r.d: Other shops' prices do not appear in the ad at all. This is a guess with no evidence to compare.
x-e-m2-02.s.s1.explain: If you buy 3, one is free, so you pay for only 2 (a), and since the condition is 'buy 2', there is no free muffin if you buy just 1 (c). A deal tomorrow (b) is the opposite of 'Today only', and a price comparison with other bakeries (d) has no basis in the ad.
x-e-m2-02.s.s2.prompt: Write in English one question that is not answered in the ad but that you would want to ask the bakery before going, and also write why you want to ask it.
x-e-m2-02.s.s2.hint.0: Reread the ad and look for a place where you think, 'This isn't written.'
x-e-m2-02.s.s2.hint.1: Picture situations such as which muffin is the free one, or what kinds you can choose from.
x-e-m2-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Is the answer to your question not already written in the ad?
x-e-m2-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Would the answer to your question change which muffins you buy or whether you go?
x-e-m2-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Does your reason connect to your question?
x-e-m2-02.s.s1.hint.1: Find the sentence in the ad that is the basis for each choice, draw a line to it, and mark the choices for which you cannot find a basis.

x-e-m2-03.title: Find a schedule that fits the conditions in a club meeting email
x-e-m2-03.goal: Read all the conditions in the email, make different schedules that meet them, and explain which conditions you checked.
x-e-m2-03.material:
This is an email from Hana, the president of a reading club, to a member, Minho. Write the days as numbers: Mon=1, Tue=2, Wed=3, Thu=4, Fri=5.

Hi Minho,
Let's plan our reading club meeting for next week.
1) We meet on a weekday, Monday to Friday, but not on Wednesday (I have a dentist visit) and not on Friday (the library closes early).
2) School ends at 3 p.m., so we can start at 3 p.m. at the earliest. The room can be used until 6 p.m.
3) The meeting takes two hours, and it always starts on the hour.
Please send me the days and start times that work.
Thanks, Hana
x-e-m2-03.thinking.0: Find answers that meet several conditions at once
x-e-m2-03.thinking.1: Explain the conditions you checked in English
x-e-m2-03.prereq.0: Read English day names and times
x-e-m2-03.prereq.1: Easy expressions like two hours and until
x-e-m2-03.s.s0.prompt: Which part of the email most limits how late the start time can be?
x-e-m2-03.s.s0.hint.0: Think about how the start time and the end time are related.
x-e-m2-03.s.s0.hint.1: Underline the sentence that directly limits the time.
x-e-m2-03.s.s0.r.a: This is a condition about days, so it does not limit the start time.
x-e-m2-03.s.s0.r.b: You read the time the room can be used until together with the length of the meeting.
x-e-m2-03.s.s0.r.c: This is a request sentence, so it does not set a limit on time.
x-e-m2-03.s.s0.explain: The end time (6 o'clock) and the meeting length (two hours) together set the latest limit for the start time. The day conditions and the request sentence do not set a limit on time.
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.prompt: Make 3 different schedules that meet all the conditions in the email. d is the day number (Mon=1 to Fri=5), and h is the start time (which hour in the afternoon, e.g., 3 means 3 p.m.).
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.hint.0: Start by crossing out the days that are 'not allowed' in the email.
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.hint.1: The end time is 'start + two hours'. Compare it with the time the room can be used until.
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.var.h: Start time (which hour in the afternoon)
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.ok.c1: It is one of Monday to Friday.
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.fail.c1: The day number must be a whole number from 1 to 5.
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.ok.c2: It is not Wednesday or Friday.
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.fail.c2: Wednesday (3) and Friday (5) are ruled out in the email.
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.ok.c3: It starts on the hour after school ends.
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.fail.c3: The start time must be on the hour at or after 3 p.m.
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.ok.c4: The room can still be used two hours later.
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.fail.c4: The meeting is two hours long, so the end time goes past the time the room can be used.
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.explain: The possible days are Mon, Tue, and Thu (1, 2, 4), and the start time is 3 or 4 o'clock. If it starts at 4, it ends at 6, which is allowed because the room can be used until 6. A 5 o'clock start ends at 7, so it is not allowed.
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.because.prompt: Pick one of your schedules and write one or two sentences in English about which conditions in the email you checked.
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.because.hint.0: Check one by one which conditions in the email your chosen schedule could run into.
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.because.hint.1: You may use a pattern like '... works because ...'.
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.because.placeholder: Example: Tuesday at 4 p.m. works because ...
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.because.selfAssess.0: Are the conditions you mentioned really in the email?
x-e-m2-03.s.s1.because.selfAssess.1: Did you check the end time too?

x-e-m2-04.title: Pick evidence that supports a claim about phones at lunch
x-e-m2-04.goal: Compare a claim with evidence, decide how far each piece of evidence supports the claim, and write what the evidence cannot show.
x-e-m2-04.material:
This is a post from a student blog.

Our school should ban phones at lunch. Phones make students lonely.

The writer has collected the evidence candidates below under this claim.
x-e-m2-04.thinking.0: Decide whether evidence supports a claim
x-e-m2-04.thinking.1: Compare the scope of the claim with the scope of the evidence
x-e-m2-04.prereq.0: Read easy English sentences (survey, and easy number expressions like '30 out of 40 students' instead of percent)
x-e-m2-04.s.s1.r.a: The survey results are directly related, but they rely on what students said.
x-e-m2-04.s.s1.r.d: It is an observation compared with a week without phones, so it is evidence in which you can see a change.
x-e-m2-04.s.s2.prompt: Which claim do the two pieces of evidence, a and d, support best?
x-e-m2-04.s.s2.hint.0: Compare the words in the evidence sentences with the words in the claim sentences, side by side.
x-e-m2-04.s.s2.r.a: 'Lonely' does not appear in the evidence. The claim is bigger than what the evidence says.
x-e-m2-04.s.s3.prompt: Pick one of a (the survey) and d (the week without phones), and write one or two sentences in English about what that evidence cannot tell you.
x-e-m2-04.s.s3.hint.0: Think about how that evidence was gathered (who, for how long, and how).
x-e-m2-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the limit you wrote really connect to the evidence you picked?
x-e-m2-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write 'what it fails to show' rather than 'it is bad evidence'?
x-e-m2-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about the possibility that there are other explanations (causes)?
x-e-m2-04.s.s1.prompt: You want to check the writer's claim "Phones make students lonely." Among the candidates below, choose all the evidence that directly shows what our school's students actually do at lunchtime.
x-e-m2-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each piece of evidence, mark which school it is about, who said it, and whether it is about lunchtime.
x-e-m2-04.s.s1.hint.1: For each piece of evidence, write in one line "what was counted or asked to get this information."
x-e-m2-04.s.s1.r.b: It is one person's story from another school, and happiness and lunchtime conversation are not the same thing.
x-e-m2-04.s.s1.r.c: That there are many phones is not evidence about what lunchtime looks like.
x-e-m2-04.s.s1.explain: a is a survey the students answered themselves, and d is an observation that counted the increase in tables where people talk during the week phones were not used. Both directly show what our school's lunchtime looks like. b mixes a different topic, happiness, into one person's story from another school, and c only states the fact that there are many phones.
x-e-m2-04.s.s2.hint.1: Find whether there is a word or range (who, where, what) that is only in the claim sentence and not in the evidence sentence.
x-e-m2-04.s.s2.r.b: This is a big claim that tries to speak for all schools from the data of one school.
x-e-m2-04.s.s2.o.c: If students use phones at lunchtime, they talk with friends less.
x-e-m2-04.s.s2.r.c: This is a claim of the same size as the range the evidence talks about.
x-e-m2-04.s.s2.explain: What the evidence shows goes only as far as "less talking at lunchtime." To go to loneliness (a) or banning at all schools (b), you need other evidence that directly supports that claim.
x-e-m2-04.s.s3.hint.1: Words like "only," "may not," and "does not show" can help.

x-e-m2-05.title: Rewrite the claim that going to the library often raises scores
x-e-m2-05.goal: Each time new data is revealed, decide again how sure you can be about the claim, and rewrite the final sentence.
x-e-m2-05.material: A blog writer wants to write this: 'Library visits make students' scores go up.' Let's check this sentence against the data.
x-e-m2-05.thinking.0: Revise your judgment with new information
x-e-m2-05.thinking.2: Adjust how strong a claim is
x-e-m2-05.prereq.0: Read easy English sentences (average, score, library visits)
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed one piece at a time. At each step, pick the most fitting judgment using only what is known so far.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, check whether the new information supports the earlier judgment or shakes it.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how 'change together' is different from 'change because of'.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: What about writing 'Library visits make scores go up' based on this data alone?
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.0.after: The data only shows that the two things move together. We still can't tell whether the library is the cause.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It has been proven that the library raises scores.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Changing together and being the cause are different.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Library visits and scores move together, but we don't yet know why.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This judgment separates a relationship of moving together from a cause.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Library visits have nothing to do with scores.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The data shows there is a relationship. Saying there is none is the opposite of the data.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.1.ask: How will your judgment change when this information is added?
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.1.after: If students who go often also have other habits, it becomes hard to separate whether the library or those habits cause the difference in scores.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Other reasons, such as homework and sleep, could explain both scores and visits.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This judgment takes the possibility of other explanations into account.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It has become clearer that the library is the cause.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The new information instead adds other explanations.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The new information does not deny the first data. It only widens the interpretation.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: How will you evaluate the original sentence with this test result?
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.2.after: The group that visited rose by only the same amount as the group that did not visit. The original sentence is not supported by this test. You can also remember that the short period is a limit.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It has been confirmed that library visits raise scores a lot.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The change in the two groups is the same, 1 point. The visiting group did not rise by much more.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.2.o.b: In this test, visiting did not make scores rise more.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This judgment comes from comparing the change in the two groups.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Four weeks is short, so we should be careful, but it does not support the original sentence.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This judgment admits the limits of the result but sees that it does not become a basis for the claim.
x-e-m2-05.s.s1.reflect: At first you could only say 'they move together'. With the second piece of information, other explanations appeared, and with the third test, the original sentence became weaker. Think about which piece of information changed your judgment.
x-e-m2-05.s.s2.prompt: Write one or two sentences in English that fit the data better than 'Library visits make students' scores go up.' and that the blog writer could use instead.
x-e-m2-05.s.s2.hint.0: Separate what you can say for sure from what you still don't know from the three pieces of data.
x-e-m2-05.s.s2.hint.1: You can use expressions that weaken a claim (may, does not prove, etc.).
x-e-m2-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does your sentence fit all three pieces of data?
x-e-m2-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is the claim weaker than the original sentence?
x-e-m2-05.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you keep the certain part (moving together)?

x-e-m2-06.title: Fix the tone of a request email to a teacher
x-e-m2-06.goal: Find the line in a request email whose tone doesn't suit the person receiving it, and rewrite it politely.
x-e-m2-06.material: This is an email from a student, Jina, to the librarian teacher. She wants to borrow the music room key to practice for the school festival. (Each line has a number.)
x-e-m2-06.thinking.0: Judge a tone that fits the receiver and the situation
x-e-m2-06.prereq.0: You have probably seen basic request expressions like please, could, and may I
x-e-m2-06.s.s1.prompt: Pick the line whose tone is least suitable for sending to the receiver (a teacher).
x-e-m2-06.s.s1.hint.0: Compare the tone of the sentence that asks for something with the greeting and reason sentences.
x-e-m2-06.s.s1.explain: Line 3 has a commanding tone ('Give me ... now.'), so it sounds rude as a request to a teacher. Line 1 is a greeting, line 2 is a self-introduction, line 4 is the reason, and line 5 is a thank-you, so all of them are suitable.
x-e-m2-06.s.s2.prompt: Pick the most suitable sentence to replace line 3.
x-e-m2-06.s.s2.hint.0: Compare the forms: is it a command, or a question asking for permission?
x-e-m2-06.s.s2.r.b: It has 'please', but it is still a command and feels threatening.
x-e-m2-06.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite line 3 politely to the teacher in English, in your own way, different from the choices above.
x-e-m2-06.s.s3.hint.0: Try starting with a question that asks for permission (Could/May/Would ...) or with 'I would like ...'.
x-e-m2-06.s.s3.hint.1: Check that your sentence says you want to borrow the key.
x-e-m2-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the tone not awkward if you were talking to a teacher?
x-e-m2-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is what you are asking for (the key) clear?
x-e-m2-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid being too long and roundabout?
x-e-m2-06.s.s1.hint.1: Write down whether each line is greeting, introduction, request, reason, or thanks, and read it aloud as if speaking to a teacher.
x-e-m2-06.s.s2.hint.1: Put each choice into an email to a teacher, read it aloud, and write down why it sounds awkward.
x-e-m2-06.s.s2.r.a: "Hey" and a casual tone suit a friend.
x-e-m2-06.s.s2.r.c: This is a polite request asking whether you may borrow it.
x-e-m2-06.s.s2.r.d: It sounds like a request that asks for permission, not one that first declares a need and only asks for agreement.
x-e-m2-06.s.s2.explain: Could I borrow ... , please? is polite because the person asking seeks the other person's permission. "Please give me ... now" is an order even with please, "Hey, can you ..." is a casual tone that suits a friend, and "I need ..." sounds like a demand because it first says what you need.
x-e-m2-06.s.s3.modelNote.3: Can you ...? is slightly more casual than Could ...? but it is a question that asks permission.

x-e-m2-07.title: Write a text message that shows nervousness without saying it
x-e-m2-07.goal: Make a short English message that lets the reader infer an emotion without saying the emotion directly.
x-e-m2-07.material: A friend is nervous about a test tomorrow and is about to send a text at night. The reader should be able to guess 'This friend is nervous', but the writer does not say the emotion directly.
x-e-m2-07.thinking.0: Tell apart what is said directly from what is only hinted
x-e-m2-07.thinking.1: Write so that the emotion comes across through clues alone
x-e-m2-07.prereq.0: Write everyday English sentences (present tense, progressive)
x-e-m2-07.prereq.1: The meanings of emotion words (nervous, worried, etc.)
x-e-m2-07.s.s1.prompt: Which of the following three messages does not state the emotion directly and lets you guess the nervousness from clues in the situation?
x-e-m2-07.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether there are clues (actions, situations) the reader can use to guess.
x-e-m2-07.s.s1.r.c: There is no clue to guess a test or nervousness.
x-e-m2-07.s.s2.prompt: Write an English message of two or three sentences that lets the reader guess that a friend is nervous about a test tomorrow. Do not use emotion words such as nervous, worried, scared, afraid, or anxious.
x-e-m2-07.s.s2.hint.0: Picture what that friend might be doing at night, or how their body feels.
x-e-m2-07.s.s2.hint.1: The message should include the test or when tomorrow is so that the reader can understand the situation.
x-e-m2-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: In your message, what are the clues the reader can use to guess the nervousness?
x-e-m2-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is the situation clear even without emotion words?
x-e-m2-07.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Does it show that the test is tomorrow?
x-e-m2-07.s.s1.hint.0: In each message, mark separately the part that directly explains the writer's feelings and what the writer is doing.
x-e-m2-07.s.s1.r.a: It directly states the feeling with "scared."
x-e-m2-07.s.s1.r.b: It has only actions and the situation, with no emotion word, but the reader can guess.
x-e-m2-07.s.s1.explain: b lets the reader guess nervousness from only the action of keep rereading the notes and the situation that the test is tomorrow. a directly has an emotion word (scared), and c has no clue to guess a test or nervousness.

x-e-m2-08.title: Decide what to ask before choosing a restaurant for a birthday dinner
x-e-m2-08.goal: Judge whether the information needed for a decision is already there or still missing, and write an English message asking for the information you need.
x-e-m2-08.material:
A friend asked you: "Recommend a restaurant near Hongik University Station where 8 people can eat Korean food on Saturday at 7 p.m."

The restaurant ad you found:
Seoul Table — Korean food. Main dishes 12,000 to 16,000 won. Open every day, 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Near Hongdae Station. Our tables seat up to 6 people.
x-e-m2-08.thinking.0: Separate information you already have from missing information
x-e-m2-08.thinking.1: Choose the questions that are really needed for the decision
x-e-m2-08.prereq.1: Numbers and English expressions for days and times
x-e-m2-08.s.s1.prompt: Which question must you ask the restaurant before recommending it?
x-e-m2-08.s.s1.hint.0: Match your friend's conditions (number of people, day, time, food, place) with the ad one by one.
x-e-m2-08.s.s1.hint.1: Mark where the conditions and the ad clash, or items that are not in the ad.
x-e-m2-08.s.s1.r.a: The fact that it is near the station is already in the ad.
x-e-m2-08.s.s2.prompt: Write an English message to send to the restaurant. Tell them the number of people, the day, and the time, and include one question that will solve the problem you found above.
x-e-m2-08.s.s2.hint.0: First write down the information the message must include (how many people, what day, what time).
x-e-m2-08.s.s2.hint.1: At the end, add one question asking whether the clashing part in the ad can be solved.
x-e-m2-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you mention all of 8 people, Saturday, and 7 o'clock?
x-e-m2-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Does it include a question that solves the ad's 'up to 6' problem?
x-e-m2-08.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is it a question a restaurant staff member could read and answer right away?
x-e-m2-08.s.s1.r.b: This is a condition the friend did not ask for. It is not essential for the recommendation decision.
x-e-m2-08.s.s1.r.c: The ad already says "every day from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m."
x-e-m2-08.s.s1.r.d: This is a question about the part where the ad's "up to 6 people" and the friend's condition (8 people) clash.
x-e-m2-08.s.s1.explain: The ad says up to 6 people per table, but the friend has 8. This part has to be resolved before you can recommend it. Being near the station and open on Saturday evening are already in the ad, and vegetarian menu was not a condition the friend asked for.

x-e-m2-09.goal: Write the same content with a different tone and form depending on the receiver, and judge which parts should change.
x-e-m2-09.thinking.0: Change the tone depending on the receiver
x-e-m2-09.thinking.1: Tell apart what must change from what to leave as it is
x-e-m2-09.s.s1.prompt: Pick all the parts of this draft that would be good to change when sending it to the teacher.
x-e-m2-09.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine how each sentence in the draft would sound to the teacher.
x-e-m2-09.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Would it not be rude if the teacher read it?
x-e-m2-09.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is there no friend-style wording mixed in?
x-e-m2-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the tone different from the one you used with the teacher?

x-e-m2-09.title: Writing a request to move a practice date differently to a teacher and to a friend
x-e-m2-09.material:
The club presentation practice is scheduled for Wednesday. But there is a school test that day, so a student wants to move the practice to Thursday. The student plans to send the draft below as it is.

'Wednesday is bad. Change it to Thursday. I have a test.'

They will send this request (1) to the club teacher Mr. Han and (2) to a friend in the same club.
x-e-m2-09.prereq.0: Suggestion expressions like Can we ...? / Could we ...?
x-e-m2-09.prereq.1: Easy words such as days of the week and test
x-e-m2-09.s.s1.hint.1: Separate the information the teacher needs to decide (the reason, the new date) from the tone (the sentence form).
x-e-m2-09.s.s1.o.a: The teacher is busy, so leave out the reason (the test) and write only briefly that we move it to Thursday.
x-e-m2-09.s.s1.r.a: If you leave out the reason, it does not convey why you want to move it, so it sounds like a one-sided demand.
x-e-m2-09.s.s1.o.b: Add a greeting and a form of address (e.g., Hello, Mr. Han).
x-e-m2-09.s.s1.r.b: This is the opening part that shows courtesy to the person receiving it.
x-e-m2-09.s.s1.o.c: Change "Change it to Thursday." into a question that asks permission (e.g., Could we ...?).
x-e-m2-09.s.s1.r.c: This is the direction of changing it into a form that asks, so the other person can decide.
x-e-m2-09.s.s1.o.d: Change only "bad" to "not good for me" and leave the rest of the sentence form as it is.
x-e-m2-09.s.s1.r.d: Even if you soften one word, if an order form like "Change it to Thursday." remains, it still sounds rude.
x-e-m2-09.s.s1.explain: To the teacher, add a greeting and a form of address (b) and change an order like "Change it to Thursday." into a question asking permission (c). The reason, the test, is information the other person needs to decide, so do not leave it out (a). If you soften only one word and leave the order form as it is (d), it still sounds rude.
x-e-m2-09.s.s2.prompt: (1) Write an English message to the teacher Mr. Han. Include a greeting, the reason you cannot do it on Wednesday, a question asking whether it is okay to move it to Thursday, and thanks.
x-e-m2-09.s.s2.hint.0: Write the greeting and the form of address first, then follow with the reason you cannot do it on Wednesday.
x-e-m2-09.s.s2.hint.1: Turn the sentence that suggests Thursday into a question that asks permission.
x-e-m2-09.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Are the reason and the new date clear?
x-e-m2-09.s.s3.prompt: (2) Write the same request as a casual English message to a friend in the same club. Keep the reason, the test, and the Thursday suggestion, but use a more relaxed tone than the one you used with the teacher.
x-e-m2-09.s.s3.hint.0: Decide which parts of the message to the teacher you want to change (greeting, form of address, question form).
x-e-m2-09.s.s3.hint.1: Keep the reason and the new date as they are.
x-e-m2-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Are the reason and the new date unchanged?

x-e-m2-10.title: Reread a friend's cancellation text as new news arrives
x-e-m2-10.goal: Each time one more piece of news is added, reinterpret the friend's cancellation text and write a fitting reply.
x-e-m2-10.material: Sora planned to see a movie with her friend Jun on Saturday. Then a text arrives from Jun.
x-e-m2-10.thinking.0: Revise your interpretation with new information
x-e-m2-10.thinking.1: Consider circumstances that were not said
x-e-m2-10.thinking.2: Write a reply that fits the situation
x-e-m2-10.prereq.1: Easy expressions like hospital and next Saturday
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.prompt: The texts are revealed one at a time. At each step, pick the most fitting interpretation using only what is known so far.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.hint.0: At this step, separate the words actually written in the text from what you guessed.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the new text supports the earlier interpretation or changes it.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.0.ask: Why is it most fitting for Sora to think Jun can't come?
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.0.after: 'Something came up' means that something has come up. The text alone cannot tell you what that is.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Something came up for Jun, but we don't know yet what it is.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This interpretation reads only as much as the text says.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.0.r.c: There is no basis to think it's a lie.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.1.ask: How will your interpretation change after receiving this text?
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.1.after: When a family member is sick, it can be hard to explain right away. You can understand why the first text was short.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Jun may have found it hard to say right away what was going on.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This interpretation uses the new information to understand the reason that was not said before.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Jun tried to hide the reason from the start.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.1.r.b: 'Tried to hide' is a judgment that is not in the new text.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Jun is not interested in movies.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The new information has nothing to do with that.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.reflect: With the first text, the only interpretation was that we don't know the reason, and the interpretation changed each time a new text came. Think about which sentence changed the interpretation, and why it was important not to make up a reason at first.
x-e-m2-10.s.s2.prompt: Write one or two English sentences as Sora's reply to the last text. Consider Jun's circumstances while also answering about the next date.
x-e-m2-10.s.s2.hint.0: Decide whether to begin with words that care about Jun's feelings first (comfort, understanding).
x-e-m2-10.s.s2.hint.1: Check that your sentences include an answer to the suggestion of next Saturday.
x-e-m2-10.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is there an answer about the next date?
x-e-m2-10.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is it free of a demanding or prying tone?
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It seems Jun has a family member who is sick.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.0.r.a: That could be, but the text has no clue to guess the reason. This is an interpretation that settles on one reason.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the most fitting direction for Sora's reply?
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.2.after: c responds to the next schedule while taking the other person's circumstances into account. a did not reflect the new information, and b did not continue the consideration that kept Jun from feeling burdened.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This has a tone that demands answers without considering the other person's circumstances.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.2.r.b: It carries concern, but it misses Jun's words "thank you for not asking too much" and keeps probing.
x-e-m2-10.s.s1.st.2.r.c: It carries both concern and acceptance of the schedule.
